content: The health burden caused by helminth infections is significant, perpetuating a cycle of infection, poverty, reduced productivity, and limited socioeconomic development. These infections can also exacerbate other conditions, such as malaria and HIV/AIDS, and hinder the effectiveness of vaccines against infectious diseases. Since the late 20th century, the recognition of the impact of helminthiases has led to the establishment of large-scale control and elimination programs targeting both the parasites and their transmission vectors or hosts. In 1975, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the World Bank, and later UNICEF, launched the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR). This initiative was followed by the creation of the Onchocerciasis Control Programme (OCP) in West Africa. Subsequent programs, such as the Onchocerciasis Elimination Program for the Americas (OEPA) in 1993 and the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC) in 1995, were also initiated. In 2000, the Global Alliance to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) was launched, aiming to treat at least 75% of school-aged children at risk of soil-transmitted helminthiases (STHs) and schistosomiasis by 2010. This effort led to the establishment of the Partners for Parasite Control (PPC) by WHO. The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) have further motivated global public health efforts, resulting in initiatives like the Schistosomiasis Control Initiative (SCI) in 2002 and the Global Network for Neglected Tropical Disease Control (GNNTDC) in 2006. Helminthic diseases, closely linked to poverty, not only arise from poverty but also contribute to it by impairing agricultural productivity, cognitive development, and education. Despite progress, challenges remain, including insufficient tools for disease mapping, sensitive diagnostics, monitoring intervention progress, assessing drug efficacy, and detecting drug resistance. Additionally, defining program endpoints and implementing post-control surveillance are critical gaps. While community engagement, environmental improvements, hygiene practices, and socioeconomic development are essential, the primary strategy for helminthiasis control has been mass drug administration (MDA). However, the limited arsenal of drugs, originally developed for veterinary use, poses a vulnerability to potential drug resistance. Long-term control and eradication will require improved sanitation, hygiene, and socioeconomic development. Helminth infections, including onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis (LF), STHs, schistosomiasis, food-borne trematodiases, and taeniasis/cysticercosis, are among the most common infectious agents in developing countries. Onchocerciasis affects 37 million people, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa, and is a leading cause of infectious blindness. LF, endemic in 83 countries, affects 120 million people, causing severe disfigurement and disability. STHs, including infections with Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and hookworms, affect over 2 billion people globally, impairing physical and cognitive development, particularly in children. Schistosomiasis, endemic in 76 countries, affects 200 million people, with 160 million cases in sub-Saharan Africa alone. It causes significant morbidity, including portal hypertension, organomegaly, and associations with liver and bladder cancers. Food-borne trematodiases, caused by liver flukes like Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis, are major public health concerns in Asia, linked to hepatobiliary diseases and cholangiocarcinoma. Taenia solium, endemic in Latin America, Asia, and Africa, causes neurocysticercosis, a leading cause of epilepsy and neurological disorders. Despite the health and socioeconomic impact of helminth infections, they have not received the same attention as diseases like HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. However, their control is essential for achieving the MDGs and fostering long-term economic growth. Sustainable control programs require national ownership, integration into health plans, and political commitment. Research priorities must address gaps in understanding the biology, epidemiology, and social determinants of helminth infections, as well as the development of new tools and strategies for control and elimination.
